p.src: Now the king leaned against his dragon throne, tears streaming like a fountain, and wept without cease until nightfall. Monkey stepped forward and cried aloud, “Why are you so utterly confused? The bodies of those Daoists lie before your very eyes: one is a tiger, one a deer, and Ram Power is an antelope. If you do not believe me, haul up the bones and look at them. What man ever had a skeleton like that? They were mountain beasts that had become spirits and conspired together to come here and harm you; but seeing that your allotted fortune was still strong, they dared not strike. Had another two years passed and your fortune declined, they would have taken your life and seized your entire realm for themselves. Fortunately, we arrived in time, destroyed the fiends, and saved your life. What have you still to weep about? Why weep? Hurry and endorse our travel document, and send us on our way.” Only after hearing this did the king come to his senses. All the civil and military officials memorialized, “The dead truly are a white deer and a yellow tiger, and those in the oil cauldron truly are a sheep’s bones. Your Majesty cannot but heed the holy monks’ words.” The king said, “Since that is so, I offer my thanks to the holy monks. It is late today.” Then he ordered, “Grand Preceptor, escort the holy monks for now to Zhiyuan Monastery. At tomorrow’s morning court, we shall open the Eastern Pavilion wide and have the Court of Imperial Entertainments prepare a pure vegetarian banquet to thank them.” And so they were escorted to the monastery to rest.

p.src: At the fifth watch the next morning, the king held court, assembled all his officials, and issued an edict: “Quickly publish proclamations recalling the monks, and post them at every gate and along every road.” Meanwhile, a splendid banquet was prepared. The king left the court in his carriage, went to the gate of Zhiyuan Monastery, invited Tripitaka and the others, and entered the Eastern Pavilion with them to attend the feast. We need say no more of it.

p.src: Now when the monks who had escaped with their lives heard of the proclamation recalling monks, they were all delighted. They entered the city to seek the Great Sage Sun and return his hairs in gratitude for his kindness. When the elder’s banquet was over, the king exchanged his travel document and, accompanied by the queen, imperial consorts, and both ranks of civil and military officials, escorted him out through the court gate. There they saw the monks kneeling by the roadside and crying, “Grandfather Great Sage Equal to Heaven, we are the monks who escaped with our lives on the sandy shore. We heard that you destroyed the fiends and delivered us, and that our king has also graciously issued a proclamation recalling monks. We have therefore come especially to return your hairs and bow in thanks for this heavenly grace.” Monkey laughed and asked, “How many of you have come?” The monks replied, “Five hundred—every last one of us.” Monkey gave his body a shake and gathered back the hairs. He said to the sovereign and his subjects, the monks and the laity, “It was indeed old Sun who freed these monks; as for the carts, old Sun worked a double-pin trick on them, drove them through the backbone, and smashed them to pieces; and it was old Sun who killed those two demon Daoists as well. Now that the fiends have been destroyed, you know at last that the Chan school possesses the Way. From now on, you must never again act recklessly or give your faith blindly. I ask you to unite the Three Teachings: honor the Buddhist monks, honor the Daoists, and nurture men of talent as well. Then I shall ensure that your realm remains secure forever.” The king obeyed his words and thanked him without end; then he escorted the Tang Monk out of the city.

p.src: Onward they went, devotedly seeking the Tripitaka, striving in cultivation to illuminate the primal truth. They traveled by day and lodged by night, drinking when thirsty and eating when hungry; before they knew it, spring was spent, summer had waned, and autumn had come again. One day, when the sky was already growing dark, the Tang Monk reined in his horse and asked, “Disciples, where shall we shelter tonight?” Monkey replied, “Master, a man who has left the household should not speak like one who lives in it.” Tripitaka asked, “What do householders do? And what do those who have left the household do?” Monkey said, “At this hour, householders have warm beds and cozy quilts, children nestled in their arms, and wives warming their feet, and they sleep at perfect ease. How could we who have left the household enjoy such things? We must travel beneath the moon and stars, feed on the wind, and lodge by the waters; where there is a road, we keep walking, and only where there is none do we stop.” Eight Rules said, “Brother, you know one side of the matter but not the other. The road is terribly steep and rugged now, and this heavy load is truly hard to carry. We must find somewhere to sleep soundly and restore our strength, so that tomorrow I can bear up under the load again; otherwise, will I not collapse from exhaustion?” Monkey said, “Let us go another stretch by moonlight and stop when we reach an inhabited place.” Having no choice, master and disciples followed Monkey onward.

p.src: Before they had gone much farther, they heard the thunderous roar of waves. Eight Rules said, “That settles it—we have reached the end of the road.” Sha Monk said, “A body of water is blocking our way.” The Tang Monk asked, “Then how are we to cross?” Eight Rules replied, “Let me test it and see how deep it is.” Tripitaka said, “Wuneng, do not talk nonsense. How can you test the depth of the water?” Eight Rules said, “Find a pebble and throw it into the middle. If it splashes up bubbles, the water is shallow; if it sinks with a deep gurgle, the water is deep.” Monkey said, “Go and try it, then.” The fool picked up a stone and threw it into the water. He heard only a gurgling sound as fish slime rose to the surface and the stone sank to the bottom. He said, “Deep, deep, deep! We cannot cross!” The Tang Monk said, “Though you have tested its depth, you still do not know how wide it is.” Eight Rules replied, “That I do not know, I do not know.” Monkey said, “Let me take a look.” What a Great Sage! He mounted his somersault cloud, sprang into the air, and peered intently. This is what he saw:

p.src: He quickly turned his cloud around, descended beside the river, and said, “Master, it is wide—far too wide! We cannot cross! With old Sun’s fiery eyes and golden pupils, I can ordinarily see a thousand li by day and discern good fortune from ill; even at night I can still see three to five hundred li. Yet now, however far I look, I cannot see the opposite bank. How could I determine its width?”

p.src: Tripitaka was greatly alarmed. Almost unable to speak, he choked out, “Disciples, what are we to do about this?” Sha Monk said, “Master, do not weep. Look—does that figure standing by the water not appear to be a man?” Monkey said, “It must be a fisherman working a lift net. Let me go and ask him.” Taking up his iron cudgel, he ran over in two or three strides and looked. Ah! It was not a man but a stone stele. On the stele were three large seal-script characters, and below them two lines containing ten smaller characters. The three large characters read “River That Reaches Heaven,” while the ten smaller ones read, “Eight hundred li across; since ancient times, few travelers have passed.” Monkey called, “Master, come and look.” When Tripitaka saw it, tears fell from his eyes, and he said, “Disciples, when I left Chang’an years ago, I thought the road to the Western Heaven would be easy. How could I have known that demons would bar the way and that mountains and rivers would stretch so endlessly far?”

p.src: Eight Rules said, “Master, listen. Where are those drums and cymbals sounding? There must be a household holding a vegetarian service. Let us go there, get some vegetarian food, ask where the ferry is, and find a boat. Then we can cross tomorrow.” Listening from horseback, Tripitaka indeed heard the sound of drums and cymbals. “Those are not Daoist instruments; they are certainly being played for a Buddhist ceremony. Let us go.” Monkey led the horse from the front, and the whole party followed the sound. There was no proper road at all. Over uneven ground they crossed the sandy flats and saw a cluster of dwellings, perhaps four or five hundred households, all of them quite well established. This is what they saw:

p.src: Tripitaka dismounted and saw a house beside the road. A banner stood outside its gate, while within lamps and candles shone brilliantly and fragrant incense smoke filled the air. Tripitaka said, “Wukong, this place is quite different from that hollow by the river. Under the eaves of a human dwelling we can shelter from the cold dew and sleep soundly without worry. None of you come with me. Let me first go to the charitable host’s door and ask for lodging. If he is willing to take me in, I shall call you over; but if he refuses, you must not make a scene. Your faces are ugly, and I fear you may frighten the people and cause trouble, leaving us with nowhere to stay after all.” The Pilgrim said, “That makes sense. Please go ahead, Master. We shall wait here.”

p.src: Only then did the elder remove his bamboo hat and bare his head. He shook out his short robe, dragged along his ringed staff, and went straight to the house. Seeing the gate half open and half closed, Tripitaka did not dare enter uninvited. He had stood there only a short while when an old man came out, prayer beads hanging from his neck and the name of Amitabha Buddha on his lips, intending to shut the gate. The elder hurriedly pressed his palms together and called aloud, “Venerable benefactor, this poor monk greets you.” Returning the greeting, the old man said, “Monk, you have come too late.” Tripitaka asked, “What do you mean?” The old man said, “You are late, and there is nothing left. Had you come earlier, my household was providing alms for monks: a full meal, three sheng of cooked rice, a length of white cloth, and ten copper coins. Why have you come only now?” Tripitaka bowed and said, “Venerable benefactor, this poor monk has not come for the alms feast.” The old man said, “If you have not come for the feast, what brings you here?” Tripitaka replied, “I am an imperial envoy from the Great Tang in the Eastern Land, journeying to the Western Heaven to fetch the scriptures. I have now reached your honored district, and night has fallen. Hearing drums and cymbals in your residence, I came especially to ask for one night’s lodging. I shall leave at daybreak.” The old man waved his hand. “Monk, a man who has left the world must not tell lies. From the Great Tang in the Eastern Land to this place is fifty-four thousand li. How could you have come all this way alone?” Tripitaka said, “Your observation is perfectly correct, venerable benefactor. But I have three young disciples who clear paths when we meet mountains, build bridges when we meet rivers, and protect this poor monk. Only with their aid have I reached this place.” The old man said, “If you have disciples, why did they not come with you?” Then he said, “Please, come in. There is room to rest in my house.” Tripitaka turned and called, “Disciples, come over here!”

p.src: The Pilgrim was impatient by nature, Eight Rules had been boorish from birth, and Friar Sand was reckless too. Hearing their master call, the three led the horse and carried the luggage, then, heedless of all else, rushed inside like a gust of wind. At the sight of them, the old man was so terrified that he fell to the ground, crying again and again, “Monsters have come! Monsters have come!” Tripitaka helped him up and said, “Do not be afraid, benefactor. They are not monsters but my disciples.” Trembling, the old man said, “How did such a handsome master come to choose such ugly disciples?” Tripitaka replied, “Though their looks are unappealing, they can subdue dragons and tame tigers, capture fiends, and seize demons.” Still half doubtful, the old man supported the Tang Monk and walked slowly onward.

p.src: Seeing the men stumble and scramble away, the three brothers clapped their hands and roared with laughter. The monks grew more terrified still. Knocking their heads against the floor in frantic bows, each concerned only with saving his own life, they all fled until not one remained.

p.src: Tripitaka supported the old man into the hall. All the lights were out, and the three disciples were still chuckling and laughing. The Tang Monk scolded them: “You wretches are utterly ill-behaved! Morning after morning I instruct you, and day after day I admonish you. The ancients said, ‘He who is good without instruction—what is he if not a sage? He who becomes good after instruction—what is he if not a worthy man? And he who remains bad even after instruction—what is he if not a fool?’ By behaving so outrageously, you show yourselves to be the lowest and most foolish of creatures. You charged through the gate with no sense of propriety, frightened our venerable host into a fall, scattered the scripture-chanting monks, and ruined the good work of this household. Will not the sin of it fall upon me?” His rebuke left them afraid to answer back. Only then did the old man believe that they were truly his disciples. He quickly turned, bowed, and said, “Reverend sir, no great harm has been done, none at all. We had just extinguished the lamps and put away the flowers, and the Buddhist service was about to end.” Eight Rules said, “Since the service is over, bring out the concluding feast, with wine and food. We shall eat and then go to sleep.” The old man called, “Bring lights! Bring lights!” When the people of the household heard him, they exclaimed in astonishment, “There were many incense sticks and candles in the hall for the scripture chanting. Why is he asking for lights again?” Several servants came out to look and found the place pitch-dark. They immediately lit torches and lanterns and crowded in together. But when they suddenly looked up and saw Eight Rules and Friar Sand, they panicked, dropped their torches, wheeled around, and shut the inner gate. They shouted toward the inner quarters, “Monsters have come! Monsters have come!”

p.src: The Pilgrim picked up a torch and lit the lamps and candles. He pulled over an armchair and invited the Tang Monk to sit in it; his brothers sat on either side, while the old man sat before them. Just as they were settling into their seats, an inner door opened and another old man came out, leaning on a staff. “What evil fiends have come by night to this charitable household of mine?” he demanded. The old man who had been sitting in front hurriedly rose and went behind the screen-door to meet him. “Brother, do not shout. They are no evil fiends, but arhats from the Great Tang in the Eastern Land who are going to fetch the scriptures. Though the disciples look fierce, they truly have ugly faces but kindly hearts.” Only then did the second old man lower his staff and exchange bows with all four travelers. When the greetings were over, he too sat before them and called, “Bring tea. Prepare a vegetarian meal.” He called several times, but the servants trembled with fear and dared not come near.

p.src: Unable to contain himself, Eight Rules asked, “Old sir, why are your servants running back and forth like this?” The old man replied, “I told them to bring a vegetarian meal and wait upon you gentlemen.” Eight Rules asked, “How many people will be serving us?” The old man answered, “Eight.” Eight Rules asked, “Which one of us are those eight to serve?” The old man said, “All four of you.” Eight Rules said, “That fair-faced master needs only one man; the hairy-faced fellow with the thunder-god’s snout needs only two; and the one with the gloomy face needs eight. As for me, I need twenty men to serve me before it will be enough.” The old man said, “From what you say, I suppose your appetite is rather large.” Eight Rules replied, “It is passably respectable.” The old man said, “We have the people, we have the people.” Calling adults and youngsters alike, he summoned some thirty or forty people.

u.src: Unable to contain himself, Eight Rules asked, “Old sir, why are your servants running back and forth like this?”
The old man replied, “I told them to bring a vegetarian meal and wait upon you gentlemen.”
Eight Rules asked, “How many people will be serving us?”
The old man answered, “Eight.”
Eight Rules asked, “Which one of us are those eight to serve?”
The old man said, “All four of you.”

Eight Rules said, “That fair-faced master needs only one man; the hairy-faced fellow with the thunder-god’s snout needs only two; and the one with the gloomy face needs eight. As for me, I need twenty men to serve me before it will be enough.”
The old man said, “From what you say, I suppose your appetite is rather large.”
Eight Rules replied, “It is passably respectable.”
The old man said, “We have the people, we have the people.”
Calling adults and youngsters alike, he summoned some thirty or forty people.

p.src: Only after hearing the exchange between the monk and the old man did everyone cease to be afraid. They set a table at the head of the room and invited the Tang Monk to take the place of honor; three tables were arranged along the two sides for his three disciples; and at a table in front sat the two old men. First they laid out vegetarian fruits and vegetables, followed by noodles, rice, refreshments, and vermicelli soup, all arranged in perfect order. Elder Tang raised his chopsticks and first recited the Sutra for Commencing a Meal. The Idiot was both a hasty eater and rather hungry. Without waiting for the Tang Monk to finish the sutra, he took a red-lacquered wooden bowl and tipped an entire bowlful of white rice into his mouth with a plop; in an instant it was gone. A young servant beside him said, “My lord has shown very poor judgment. Steamed buns may be tucked into one’s robe, but why tuck away rice? Won’t it soil your clothes?” Bajie laughed. “I didn’t tuck it away. I ate it.” The servant said, “You never even opened your mouth. How could you have eaten it already?” Bajie said, “You lads are the liars. I plainly ate it. If you don’t believe me, I’ll eat another and show you.” The young servants brought another bowl, filled it, and handed it to Bajie. The Idiot gave it a shake, tipped it into his mouth, and it too was gone. When the servants saw this, they cried, “Good heavens, sir! Your throat must be built of polished bricks—it is truly smooth and slippery!” Before the Tang Monk had finished his single sutra, five or six bowls had already passed through Bajie’s hands. Only then did they all raise their chopsticks and begin the vegetarian meal together. The Idiot cared nothing whether it was rice, noodles, fruit, or refreshments; he merely scooped up everything and wolfed it down, all the while shouting, “More rice! More rice!” Gradually, however, no more food appeared. Wukong called out, “Brother, eat a little less. This is still better than going hungry in a mountain hollow. Be content if you can get half full.” Bajie said, “What nonsense! As the saying goes, ‘Better to bury a monk alive than feed him without filling his belly.’” Wukong ordered, “Clear away the dishes and utensils. Pay no attention to him.” The two old men bowed and said, “To tell you the truth, my lords, we would not be concerned during the day. Even an elder with a belly as large as this one’s could be fed along with a hundred or so others. But it was late, and after the remnants of the feast had been gathered, we had prepared only one dan of noodles, five dou of rice, and several tables of vegetarian dishes, intending to invite a few relatives and neighbors and the assembled monks to share in the blessings. We never expected your company to arrive. You frightened all the monks away, and we dared not even invite our relatives and neighbors, so everything was offered to you. If you are not yet full, we shall have more steamed.” Bajie said, “Have more steamed! Have more steamed!”

p.src: When he had finished speaking, the dishes and tables were cleared away. Tripitaka bowed, thanked them for the meal, and then asked, “What is your honored surname, venerable benefactor?” The old man replied, “Chen.” Tripitaka joined his palms. “Then you belong to the same clan as this poor monk.” The old man asked, “Is your surname Chen too, my lord?” Tripitaka said, “Yes. My lay family’s surname is also Chen. May I ask what observance you were holding just now?” Bajie laughed. “Why ask him, Master? Surely you already know. It must have been a feast for the young crops, a feast for peace, or a thanksgiving feast after the harvest.” The old man said, “No, no.” Tripitaka asked again, “Then what exactly was it for?” The old man replied, “It was a funeral feast prepared in advance.” Bajie laughed so hard that he stumbled. “Old sir, you have little discernment. We are masters at spinning lies and building bridges of deceit to hoodwink people. How can you hope to deceive us with such a falsehood? Do you think monks know nothing of religious feasts? There are feasts prepared in advance to store merit in the treasury of the afterlife, and feasts prepared in advance to repay karmic debts—but who ever heard of a ‘funeral feast prepared in advance’? No one in your household has died, so why hold a funeral feast?”

p.src: Hearing this, Wukong was secretly pleased. “The Idiot has grown a little sharper. Old sir, you must have misspoken. Why do you call it a ‘funeral feast prepared in advance’?” The two old men leaned forward and said, “If you are journeying to fetch scriptures, why did you not follow the proper road? How did you stray into this place?” Wukong replied, “We did follow the proper road, but a broad river blocked our way and we could not cross. Then we heard drums and cymbals, so we came expressly to your residence to ask for lodging.” The old man asked, “When you reached the water’s edge, did you see anything?” Wukong replied, “We saw only a stone stele bearing the three characters ‘River of Heaven,’ and beneath them the ten characters, ‘Eight hundred li from end to end; since ancient times few have passed.’ There was nothing else.” The old man said, “If you had walked a little farther along the upper bank, scarcely a li from that stele, you would have found a temple to the Great King of Miraculous Power. Did you not see it?” Wukong replied, “We did not. Please tell me, old sir, what is miraculous about him?” The two old men both shed tears and said, “My lord, that Great King—

p.src: Wukong asked, “Does he demand boys and girls to eat?” The old man replied, “Precisely.” Wukong asked, “I suppose it is your household’s turn?” The old man replied, “This year it is indeed our household’s turn. There are one hundred households living here. This place lies under the jurisdiction of Yuanhui County in the Kingdom of Cart-Slow and is called Chen Family Village. Once each year a sacrifice is held for the Great King, and we must offer him one boy, one girl, pigs, sheep, sacrificial animals, and wine. He devours it all at one meal, and in return ensures that winds and rains come in due season; but if we do not hold the sacrifice, he brings calamity and disaster upon us.” Wukong asked, “How many sons do you have in your household?” The old man beat his breast. “Alas, alas! How can you speak of sons? The question fills us with shame. This man is my younger brother, named Chen Qing. I myself am called Chen Cheng. I am sixty-three this year and he is fifty-eight, and both of us have had great difficulty having children. At fifty I still had no child. My relatives and friends urged me to take a concubine, so at last, having no other recourse, I found one. She bore me a daughter, who has only just turned eight this year, and I named her One Scale of Gold.” Bajie said, “What a precious name! Why is she called One Scale of Gold?” The old man replied, “Because it was so hard for me to have children, I repaired bridges and roads, built temples and pagodas, gave alms, and fed monks. I kept an account recording where I spent three taels and where I spent five. By the year my daughter was born, I happened to have spent thirty jin of gold. Thirty jin make one scale-weight, so I called her One Scale of Gold.” Wukong asked, “And whose son is it?” The old man replied, “My younger brother has a son, also born of a concubine. He is seven this year and is named Chen Guanbao.” Wukong asked, “Why was he given that name?” The old man replied, “Our household worships the Holy Lord Guan. As this son was granted in answer to prayers made before Lord Guan’s shrine, he was named Guanbao. My brother and I have a combined age of one hundred and twenty-one, yet these are the only two descendants we have. Unexpectedly, the turn to provide the sacrifice has fallen to our household, and so we dare not withhold them. Because a parent’s love makes parting so hard, we first held a rite to ensure the children’s rebirth in a better world. That is why we call it a ‘funeral feast prepared in advance.’”

p.src: When Tripitaka heard this, tears streamed uncontrollably down his cheeks, and he said, “Just as the ancients said: ‘The ripe plum stays while the green plum falls; Heaven is especially cruel to the childless.’” Wukong laughed and said, “Let me ask him another question. Good sir, how extensive is your estate?” The two old men replied, “A fair amount: forty or fifty qing of irrigated fields, sixty or seventy qing of dry fields, and eighty or ninety tracts of pasture; two or three hundred water buffalo and yellow cattle, twenty or thirty donkeys and horses, and countless pigs, sheep, chickens, and geese. Our household also has stores of old grain we cannot finish eating and clothes we cannot wear out. All our property and holdings amount to quite a sum.” Wukong said, “With an estate like this, you must have built it up by being very thrifty.” The old man asked, “What makes you think I am thrifty?” Wukong replied, “Since you possess all this wealth, why would you bear to sacrifice your own children? If you spent fifty taels of silver, you could buy a boy; if you spent a hundred taels, you could buy a girl. Even with incidental expenses, it would be no more than two hundred taels. Then you could preserve your own children and descendants. Would that not be better?” The two old men said through their tears, “Reverend sir, you do not understand. The Great King is wondrously perceptive and often moves among our households.” Wukong asked, “When he comes among you, what does he look like? How tall is he?” The two old men replied, “We never see his form. We merely smell a gust of fragrant wind and know that Grandfather Great King has arrived. At once we burn whole measures of incense, and young and old alike bow toward the wind. He knows every last detail of our households, down to which spoons are large and which bowls are small; he even remembers the year and month in which every old and young person was born. He will accept only our own natural-born children. Never mind having nowhere to buy such children for two or three hundred taels—even with tens of millions of taels, we could never buy two children exactly like ours, born in the same year and month.”

p.src: Wukong said, “So that is how it is. Very well, then. Bring out your son and let me have a look at him.” Chen Qing hurried inside, carried Guanbao out into the hall, and set him before the lamp. Knowing nothing of life or death, the child had both sleeves stuffed with fruit and skipped about, eating and playing. Seeing him, Wukong silently recited a spell, shook himself, and transformed into the exact likeness of Guanbao. The two children took each other by the hand and danced before the lamp. The old man was so frightened that he hastily fell to his knees. The Tang Monk said, “Good sir, this is most improper, most improper.” The old man said, “This reverend gentleman was speaking just now; how did he suddenly become identical to my son, so that when I call, both answer and both come? This will shorten our lives! Please resume your true form, please resume your true form.” Wukong wiped a hand across his face and revealed his true form. Kneeling before him, the old man said, “So you truly possess such powers, reverend sir.” Wukong laughed and asked, “Did I look like your son?” The old man replied, “Yes, yes, yes! The very same face, the very same voice, the very same clothes, and the very same height.” Wukong said, “You still have not examined me closely enough. Bring a scale and weigh us. Am I not exactly his weight as well?” The old man said, “Yes, yes, yes, exactly the same weight.” Wukong asked, “Would one such as this pass as the sacrifice?” The old man replied, “Perfectly, perfectly! You would pass without question.”

p.src: Wukong said, “Today I shall take this child's place and save his life, preserving your family line and descendants. I shall go and be offered to that Great King.” Chen Qing knelt and kowtowed, saying, “Reverend sir, if your compassion truly moves you to take his place, I shall present a thousand taels of silver to Master Tang as travel expenses for his journey to the Western Heaven.” Wukong said, “And will you not thank old Monkey?” The old man replied, “Once you have taken his place as the sacrifice, you will be gone.” Wukong asked, “Why should I be gone?” The old man replied, “The Great King will eat you.” Wukong said, “Would he dare eat me?” The old man said, “If he does not eat you, surely it will only be because he finds you too rank.” Wukong laughed and said, “I shall leave it to Heaven's decree. If he eats me, my allotted life was short; if he does not, that will be my good fortune. I shall go as your sacrifice.”

p.src: Chen Qing kept kowtowing in gratitude and further promised a gift of five hundred taels of silver. Chen Cheng alone neither kowtowed nor offered thanks, but leaned against the screen door and wept bitterly. Wukong understood why. He went over, seized him, and said, “Elder brother, you neither consent nor thank me. I suppose you cannot bear to part with your daughter?” Only then did Chen Cheng kneel and say, “Yes, I cannot bear it. It is more than enough that your great kindness should save my nephew by taking his place. But I am an old man without a son and have only this one daughter. After I die, she alone will mourn me with all her heart. How could I bear to give her up?” Wukong said, “Quickly steam five dou of rice and prepare some fine vegetarian dishes for that long-snouted master of mine. Have him transform into your daughter, and the two of us brothers will go together as the sacrifices. We might as well perform a hidden act of virtue and save both your children. What do you say?”

p.src: When Bajie heard this, he was greatly alarmed and said, “Brother, if you want to show off your powers without caring whether I live or die, why must you drag me into it?” Wukong said, “Dear brother, as the saying goes, ‘Even a chicken will not eat food it has not earned.’ When we entered this house, we gratefully accepted their generous vegetarian feast, yet you complained that you had not eaten your fill. Why will you not help this family in its distress?” Bajie said, “Brother, transformations are the one thing I cannot manage.” Wukong said, “You possess thirty-six transformations yourself. How can you say you cannot?” Tripitaka called out, “Wuneng, what your elder brother says is entirely right and most appropriate. As the saying goes, ‘Saving one life is a greater merit than building a seven-storied pagoda.’ For one thing, we should repay their generous hospitality; for another, we should accumulate hidden virtue; and besides, there is nothing else to do on this cool night. You two brothers may as well go and enjoy yourselves.” Bajie said, “Just listen to Master! I can turn into a mountain, a tree, a rock, a mangy elephant, a water buffalo, or a great fat fellow easily enough; but transforming into a little girl will be rather difficult.”

p.src: Wukong said, “Elder brother, do not believe him. Bring out your daughter and let us see her.” Chen Cheng hurried inside and carried the child Yichengjin into the hall. Every member of the family—wives, concubines, adults, and children, old and young, servants and kin alike—came out to kowtow and bow, begging only that the child's life be saved. On her head the girl wore a jeweled floral coronet adorned with the Eight Treasures and dangling pearls; she wore a yellow-glinting red silk jacket, over which was a mandarin-green satin cape with a chequered collar; around her waist was tied a bright-red figured-silk skirt; on her feet was a pair of pale-red silk shoes with toad-shaped toes; and on her legs she wore two gold-embroidered gauze knee breeches. She too was holding fruit and eating it. Wukong said, “Bajie, this is the girl. Quickly transform to look like her, and we shall go as the sacrifices.” Bajie said, “Brother, how can I transform into something so tiny and delicate?” Wukong shouted, “Hurry up, unless you want a beating!” Bajie panicked and said, “Brother, do not hit me! Let me transform and see how it goes.”

p.src: The fool recited an incantation, shook his head several times, and cried, “Transform!” His head truly changed, taking on the features of a young girl; but his belly remained huge and ungainly, and the rest of him looked nothing like one. The Pilgrim laughed. “Change some more.” “You may as well beat me,” said Bajie. “I cannot change any further—what am I to do?” “Surely you cannot go with a maid’s head on a monk’s body?” said the Pilgrim. “What are we to do with you looking neither male nor female?” “Now walk the steps of the Dipper.” He breathed a mouthful of immortal breath upon him, and at once Bajie’s body changed to look exactly like the child’s. He then instructed them, “You two elders, take your esteemed wives, your sons, and your daughters inside, and be careful not to confuse anyone. “Before long my brother may try to shirk the work and sneak inside; then it will be hard to tell them apart. “Give the children good fruit to eat, and do not let them cry out, lest the Great King notice and word of our plan leak out. “Now let the two of us go and have our sport.”

p.src: The noble Great Sage instructed Wujing to protect the Tang Monk. “I shall turn into Chen Guanbao, and Bajie will turn into Yichengjin.” When both were fully prepared, they asked, “How are we to be offered? “Are we to be trussed up or tied up? “Are we to be steamed whole or chopped into pieces?” “Brother,” said Bajie, “do not play tricks on me. I have no such powers as yours.” “We would not dare, we would not dare,” said the elder. “We simply use two red-lacquered offering trays and invite you both to sit upon them. We place each tray on a table, have two young men carry each table, and bear you up to the temple.” “Good, good, good!” said the Pilgrim. “Bring out the trays and let us try them.” The elder immediately brought out two red trays, and the Pilgrim and Bajie sat upon them. Four young men lifted the two tables, carried them around the courtyard for a while, then brought them back and set them down in the hall. Delighted, the Pilgrim said, “Bajie, if we are carried about and entertained like this, then we too are monks worthy of being served on platters.” “If they carry us out and then bring us back,” said Bajie, “they may carry us back and forth until dawn for all I care. “But once they carry us to the temple, we shall be eaten. That is no game!” “Just keep your eye on me,” said the Pilgrim. “If they start to eat me, you may run.” “But who knows how he eats them?” said Bajie. “If he eats the boy first, I can easily escape; “but if he eats the girl first, what am I to do?” The elder said, “Every year during the sacrifice, some bold fellows here hide behind the temple or beneath the offering table to watch. They have seen him eat the boy first and the girl afterward.” “What luck! What luck!” said Bajie.

p.src: While the brothers were still talking, they suddenly heard a thunderous din of gongs and drums outside and saw the blaze of lanterns. The villagers opened the front gate and cried, “Bring out the virgin boy and girl!” The elder wept bitterly as the four young men carried the two of them outside.
